Well, I've had a couple encounters with challenging behavior in children, and they've all been at different ages and stages of development, so I can share a few. So I have had, I'll share one from the infant-toddler side and then one from pre-K, TK, H. From infant-toddler side, I had worked in on-demand child care, and on-demand child care is very unpredictable for children. It's not very consistent because it was just dropping random children, so it wasn't ever the same group. And I had one child who had joined, and it was their first week. They were having a very hard time, and what I noticed with them is, of course, they were very dysregulated, not knowing the space. But it was a lot of... It was a lot of new children that they weren't able to connect with. They are all infants and toddlers, so there needs to be a base of security before they are able to branch out socially and emotionally and connect with other people, including children. And in that room, I was the full-time lead teacher, and what I had done was, on the first day when I did notice those sad feelings, I communicated with mom, and I had talked to her. And I mainly asked a lot of... I gave questions on, like, interests and needs, and I observed him to see where... What areas he would play in, where would he be where he could find that sense of calm, this child. And luckily, the classroom was small, I had a small team, and I had built that relationship with that family in the short time that I had them. And we worked a lot in partnership. I did invite mom to... Let me know of any, like, books, videos, things that maybe they watch at home or things that they do at home that maybe I can integrate into the classroom, and I shared with her tips and tricks that I've used in the classroom to see which ones she's already doing or which ones are things that maybe she hasn't thought about because these are behaviors that he... She was also seeing at home from him, where he'd just get frequently dysregulated. So with that child, I did make more opportunities. For him to get more sensory input and big body play. So just to kind of meet that need, because it felt like what I observed from him is he's just looking for someone to feel secure and connect with. And because infants and toddlers don't communicate the same way we do, where we have this sophisticated built language, they're still learning. So I tried my best to do... What is it? Do primary caregiving. Where each child... Each child has a primary caregiver that meets their needs. And so we did primary caregiving with a twist where there was the primary, which was me, and then I had a co-primary, which was another teacher who was there for the full day with him. And so what we did was we both... We were both together doing care practices with him to make sure that when there are these moments where you are vulnerable, like in diapering and napping, bodily and feeding, there... He's seeing the two people that are going to be his secure base on top of the other teachers that were in the classroom. And I also invited mom to bring a photo of family. And we had put it up in the classroom alongside with all the other children's photos who were able to share, as well as anything that maybe would make him feel comfortable, like his favorite toy or favorite books, to make those accommodations for him to make him a little bit more comfortable. And over time, he did get more comfortable being in the classroom. The primary, co-primary caregiving did work for him. And it worked for us, as well, because to be honest, working with infants and toddlers, and I'm sure you know, when you are implementing something, it has to be something that's sustainable, so that way infants and toddlers can feel secure. And if he had the primary, which is just one person, it would be a challenge for days where, let's say, that primary is not there and that secure base is gone. So doing the co-primary approach with him really worked for the days where, let's say, I wasn't in the classroom and needed to do a lead meeting, or the other teacher wasn't available, so I was there. So it was really a lot of collaboration and partnership, not just with the team, but with the family. But that's the perspective from the infant-toddler side. Pre-K, TK side, of course, it's very different. Oh, no worries. Thanks. Bye.
